lines.text: A green Sahara, Greek and Roman cities by the sea, colonial rule, a king, a colonel, and a long war. This is the story of Libya.
In the mountains of Tadrart Acacus, people painted the rocks thousands of years ago, when the Sahara was still green.
On the coast, Leptis Magna began as a trading post and grew into one of the grandest cities of Roman Africa, its ruins still standing.
Phoenician traders also founded Tripoli, a harbour that would become the capital.
In the east grew silphium, a plant so prized for cooking and medicine that it went on the coins, until it was harvested to extinction.
Greek settlers founded Cyrene in the east, a city that grew rich on that very plant.
Septimius Severus was born at Leptis Magna. He became Roman emperor, founded a dynasty, and died far away at York in Britain.
After Arab conquest and centuries of Ottoman rule, Italy invaded in 1911. Omar Mukhtar led the resistance for twenty years, until he was hanged in 1931.
Idris, leader of the Senussi order, was born. He would become the country's first and only king.
Italy joined its provinces into a single colony, Italian Libya, which it held until the Second World War.
In 1942 Muammar Gaddafi was born in the desert near Sirte. He would rule Libya for more than forty years.
In 1951 Libya became independent, a kingdom under Idris. Soon oil was found beneath its sands.
In 1969 a group of young officers led by Gaddafi overthrew the king and ended the monarchy.
Gaddafi began the Great Man-Made River, vast pipes carrying ancient water from under the Sahara to the coast.
In 2011 an uprising, backed by foreign air power, overthrew Gaddafi, and he was killed.
Peace did not follow. By 2014 rival governments in the east and west were at war.
Then in September 2023, Storm Daniel burst two dams above Derna, and thousands died in a single night.
Ancient, rich and divided, Libya is still waiting for its next chapter of peace.
